title: Weathering and Erosion
seo_title: Grade 5 Science: Weathering and Erosion Worksheets (MATATAG)
standard_text: Weathering breaks rocks into smaller pieces; erosion carries the pieces away by water, wind and ice; deposition builds new land; people can protect land from erosion. (summary of the MATATAG Science curriculum, Grade 5, Quarter 4: Earth and Space)
meta_desc: Free Grade 5 Science worksheets (MATATAG, Quarter 4: Earth and Space): weathering, erosion and deposition, fast and slow changes, protecting land and erosion investigations. 100 questions with answers.
key_big: Weathering breaks rock; erosion moves it.
key_sub: Water, wind, ice and living things shape the land, slowly or quickly.
body_html:
How to think about it

Weathering breaks rocks into smaller pieces. Heat from the Sun and cooling at night, rain, plant roots and burrowing animals all break rock and soil. Some chemicals in water slowly dissolve rock.

Erosion carries the broken pieces away by running water, waves and wind; deposition drops them in a new place, building beaches, deltas and sandbars. Heavy rain on bare slopes can cause soil erosion and landslides, so people plant trees and grass to hold the soil.

Example

Plant roots grow into a crack in a rock. What happens?

roots push as they grow

Answer: the rock breaks

Example

Is a landslide a fast or slow change?

it happens in seconds

Answer: fast

Common mistakes

  • Mixing up weathering (breaking) and erosion (moving).
  • Thinking erosion only happens by water.
  • Thinking land never changes.

faq.q: What is the difference between weathering and erosion?
faq.a: Weathering breaks rock down. Erosion moves the broken pieces to a new place.

faq.q: How did the Chocolate Hills of Bohol form?
faq.a: They are limestone hills shaped over a very long time by weathering and erosion by rain and running water.

faq.q: How can we stop soil erosion?
faq.a: By planting trees and grass, building terraces and walls, and not removing plants from slopes.

items.q: Which change to the land takes the longest?
c: a river carving a deep valley
items.e: River valleys form over thousands of years.

items.q: Which of these is caused by deposition?
c: a sandbar at the mouth of a creek
a cliff falling into the sea
items.e: A sandbar forms where sand is dropped.

items.q: Which helps stop soil erosion on a hillside?
items.e: Roots hold soil in place.

items.q: A glacier carries boulders as it slowly moves down a valley. Which process is this?
items.e: Transportation carries the pieces to a new place.

items.q: Which change is usually slowest?
c: a storm washing away a beach
items.e: Weathering by wind can take thousands of years.

items.q: After a flood, a layer of mud is left on the farm paddocks. Which process is this?
items.e: Deposition drops the pieces when the water, wind or ice slows down.

items.q: A fast creek scrapes sand and pebbles from its banks. Which process is this?
items.e: Erosion picks up and removes rock pieces and soil.

items.q: What is erosion?
c: the moving of soil and rock pieces by water, wind or ice
the breaking of rock in place only
items.e: Erosion carries sediment away.

items.q: What is weathering?
c: the breaking down of rock into smaller pieces
dropping sediment in a new place
items.e: Weathering breaks; erosion moves.

items.q: Which change happens fastest?
items.e: Some changes take minutes; others take thousands of years.

items.q: A river slows down where it meets the sea and drops mud, forming new land. Which process is this?
items.e: Deposition drops the pieces when the water, wind or ice slows down.

items.q: A muddy river carries soil many kilometers downstream. Which process is this?
items.e: Transportation carries the pieces to a new place.

items.q: Layers of sand settle at the bottom of a lake over many years. Which process is this?
items.e: Deposition drops the pieces when the water, wind or ice slows down.

items.q: Wind drops sand behind a fence and a small dune forms. Which process is this?
items.e: Deposition drops the pieces when the water, wind or ice slows down.

items.q: Kevin finds photos of a cliff taken 50 years apart that look almost the same. Is this evidence of a fast change or a slow change?
items.e: The cliff barely changed in 50 years.

items.q: Joy finds an old photo of a big rock and a new photo of the same rock, only a bit smaller after 100 years. Is this evidence of a fast change or a slow change?
items.e: It took 100 years to change a little.

items.q: What can farmers plant to reduce wind erosion?
items.e: Windbreaks slow the wind.

items.q: What is a glacier?
c: a huge, slow-moving body of ice
items.e: Glaciers erode the land as they move.

items.q: A river bank is wearing away near a farm. Which solution would help most?
c: remove the plants on the bank
plant shrubs and trees along the bank
items.e: Roots hold soil.

items.q: Cattle trample a riverbank and the soil is washed away. Which process is this?
items.e: Erosion picks up and removes rock pieces and soil.

items.q: A cliff is changed by weathering, erosion, transportation and deposition. Which step usually comes second?
items.e: The usual order: weathering, erosion, transportation, deposition.

items.q: A cliff is changed by weathering, erosion, transportation and deposition. Which step usually comes first?
items.e: The usual order: weathering, erosion, transportation, deposition.

items.q: A river carries mud out to sea after heavy rain. What is mainly causing this change?
items.e: The cause of this change is running water.

items.q: Red dust from a dry paddock blows over a city. What is mainly causing this change?
items.e: The cause of this change is wind.

items.q: Plant roots grow into cracks in rocks. What kind of weathering is this?
items.e: Roots can split rocks.

items.q: Why do farmers plant rows of trees between fields?
c: to slow the wind and reduce soil erosion
items.e: Windbreaks protect soil.

items.q: Rocks fall down a steep slope after heavy rain loosens them. What is mainly causing this change?
items.e: The cause of this change is gravity.

items.q: A cliff is changed by weathering, erosion, transportation and deposition. Which step usually comes third?
items.e: The usual order: weathering, erosion, transportation, deposition.

items.q: Why do rocks in a fast river become smooth and round?
c: They bump and rub against each other as the water carries them.
items.e: Moving water erodes rock.

items.q: Ocean waves crash against a rocky shore. What happens to the rocks over time?
c: They are broken and smoothed into pebbles and sand.
items.e: Waves are an agent of erosion.

items.q: Loose soil slides down a hillside cut for a new road. What is mainly causing this change?
items.e: The cause of this change is gravity.

items.q: Floodwater digs out the bank of a creek on a bend. What is mainly causing this change?
items.e: The cause of this change is running water.

items.q: Sand dunes slowly move inland across the coast. What is mainly causing this change?
items.e: The cause of this change is wind.

items.q: Where does a river drop most of its sediment?
c: at the top of a waterfall
where it slows down, like at its mouth
items.e: Slow water cannot carry as much.

items.q: Rain running off a parking lot cuts a channel in the dirt beside it. What is mainly causing this change?
items.e: The cause of this change is running water.

items.q: Which process mainly formed the Twelve Apostles in Victoria?
c: weathering and erosion by wind and rain
items.e: Waves eroded the limestone cliffs, leaving stacks of rock.

items.q: Which process mainly formed Kings Canyon in the Northern Territory?
items.e: Water and weathering cut deep into the sandstone.

items.q: Which agent of erosion shaped the sand dunes at Sandbanks Provincial Park?
items.e: Wind moves sand into dunes.

items.q: Sand blasts against a rock in a dust storm and smooths it. What is mainly causing this change?
items.e: The cause of this change is wind.

items.q: A cliff is changed by weathering, erosion, transportation and deposition. Which step usually comes last?
items.e: The usual order: weathering, erosion, transportation, deposition.

items.q: Rafael looks at this picture. This storm floods a town. How long does it take?
items.e: It is a fast change.

items.q: Nico compares a rock falling off a cliff and a cave forming. Which happens faster?
c: a rock falling off a cliff
items.e: A rock falling off a cliff takes seconds; a cave forming takes thousands of years.

items.q: Isabel reads: “Tree roots crack a big rock.” How long does this usually take?
items.e: This is a slow change: many years.

items.q: Dennis reads: “Tree roots crack a big rock.” Is this a fast change or a slow change?
c: It happens every day in every town.
items.e: It takes many years, so it is slow.

items.q: Jomar reads: “A tall mountain wears down and gets shorter.” How long does this usually take?
items.e: This is a slow change: millions of years.

items.q: Patricia compares a rock wearing into sand and an earthquake. Which happens slower?
items.e: A rock wearing into sand takes thousands of years; an earthquake takes seconds or minutes.

items.q: Angelo compares an earthquake and mud turning into rock. Which happens faster?
items.e: An earthquake takes seconds or minutes; mud turning into rock takes millions of years.

items.q: Camille looks at this picture. Wind and rain wear down this mountain. Is it a fast change or a slow change?
items.e: It takes millions of years.

items.q: What is deposition?
c: dropping eroded sediment in a new place
items.e: Rivers drop sand where they slow down.

items.q: Kenneth reads: “Layers of mud pile up and turn into rock.” Is this a fast change or a slow change?
c: It happens every day in every town.
items.e: It takes millions of years, so it is slow.

items.q: Why are retaining walls built on steep slopes?
c: to hold soil and rock in place
items.e: Walls reduce landslides.

items.q: Nico looks at this picture. This volcano erupts. How long does it take?
items.e: It is a fast change.

items.q: Lance looks at this picture. This volcano erupts. Is it a fast change or a slow change?
items.e: It takes hours or days.

items.q: Arnel reads: “Ocean waves wear away a rocky cliff.” Is this a fast change or a slow change?
c: It happens every day in every town.
items.e: It takes hundreds of years, so it is slow.

items.q: Diane looks at this picture. Wind and rain wear down this mountain. How long does it take?
items.e: It is a slow change.

items.q: Jasmine reads: “A tall mountain wears down and gets shorter.” Is this a fast change or a slow change?
c: It happens every day in every town.
items.e: It takes millions of years, so it is slow.

items.q: Hazel compares a mountain wearing down and a storm wave hitting a dune. Which happens slower?
c: a storm wave hitting a dune
items.e: A mountain wearing down takes millions of years; a storm wave hitting a dune takes hours.

items.q: Lance compares a flood and a river carving a canyon. Which happens slower?
items.e: A river carving a canyon takes millions of years; a flood takes hours or days.

items.q: Angel compares a landslide and a rock wearing into sand. Which happens faster?
items.e: A landslide takes minutes; a rock wearing into sand takes thousands of years.

items.q: Diane reads: “A landslide sends mud and rocks down a hill.” How long does this usually take?
items.e: This is a fast change: minutes.

items.q: Vincent finds a book that says the canyon took millions of years to form. Is this evidence of a fast change or a slow change?
items.e: Millions of years is very slow.

items.q: Ella finds a video of mud sliding over a road in 1 minute. Is this evidence of a fast change or a slow change?
items.e: It happened in 1 minute.

items.q: Ella builds two model sand dunes. She covers one with spinifex grass cuttings and blows a fan at both. What is she testing?
items.e: The plants are the variable she changed.

items.q: Where can you find out about Earth changes?
items.e: Use more than one source.

items.q: Jenny photographs a creek bank every month for a year. The bank moves back 40 cm. Which question does this answer?
c: What will the weather be tomorrow?
How fast is the creek eroding its bank?
How many fish live in the creek?
items.e: Repeated photos measure slow change.

items.q: A beach lost 3 m of sand in a big storm. Over the next 6 months it gained 1 m back each 2 months. How wide is it now compared with before the storm?
items.e: Erosion in the storm, deposition afterwards: 1 m × 3 = 3 m.

items.q: Can a slow change still change the land a lot?
c: Yes, over a very long time.
items.e: Slow does not mean small.

items.q: Kenneth blows through a straw at a pile of sand and gravel. What does he see?
c: The gravel moves further than the sand.
The fine sand moves further than the gravel.
items.e: Wind can carry light pieces further.

items.q: Nicole finds a video of lava pouring down a volcano in one night. Is this evidence of a fast change or a slow change?
items.e: It happened in one night.

items.q: Which change happens very quickly?
c: a glacier wearing down a mountain
items.e: Some changes take seconds, others take millions of years.

items.q: What can a volcano do in a few hours?
items.e: Eruptions are fast.

items.q: Jasmine finds a scientist's report that a rockslide closed a trail in a few seconds. Is this evidence of a fast change or a slow change?
items.e: It took seconds.

items.q: Which change is slow?
items.e: Canyons take millions of years.

items.q: Kristine pours 500 mL of water on two trays of soil. One is bare; one has grass. The bare tray loses 120 g of soil. Which result is most likely for the grass tray?
items.e: Grass roots hold the soil.

items.q: A stream table has water flowing on a gentle slope. Where will most sand be dropped?
c: at the top, where the water starts
in the middle of the fastest part
at the bottom, where the water spreads out and slows
items.e: Slow water deposits sand.

items.q: In a stream table, which change would carry the most sand away?
c: a flatter slope and less water
a steeper slope and more water
the same slope and no water
items.e: Faster water erodes and carries more.

items.q: What does 'weathering' mean?
c: rock slowly breaking into smaller pieces
items.e: Wind, water and ice break rock.

items.q: Which variable should stay the same when testing how slope affects erosion?
c: the amount of soil washed away
items.e: Only the slope should change.

items.q: How long can a big canyon take to form?
items.e: Rivers cut rock very slowly.

items.q: Which change is fast?
items.e: Earthquakes last seconds or minutes.

items.q: Bea's photo from 1950 and her photo from today show the same cliff, almost the same. What kind of change is the cliff having?
items.e: Very little change in many years.

items.q: Strong wind picks up loose sand from a dune. Which process is this?
items.e: Erosion picks up and removes rock pieces and soil.

items.q: Water seeps into a crack in a rock, freezes, expands and splits the rock. Which process is this?
items.e: Weathering breaks rock into smaller pieces where it is.

items.q: A huge chunk of a cliff collapses onto the beach below. What is mainly causing this change?
items.e: The cause of this change is gravity.

items.q: Why does bare soil erode more than soil covered by grass?
c: Roots hold the soil and leaves slow the rain.
items.e: Plants protect soil.

items.q: Sand settles on the inside bend of a river where the water is slow. Which process is this?
items.e: Deposition drops the pieces when the water, wind or ice slows down.

items.q: Lichen growing on a rock slowly breaks down its surface. Which process is this?
items.e: Weathering breaks rock into smaller pieces where it is.

items.q: Pebbles on a beach are rolled smooth by the sea. What is mainly causing this change?
items.e: The cause of this change is waves.

items.q: Fine sand is blown off a plowed field on a windy day. What is mainly causing this change?
items.e: The cause of this change is wind.

items.q: A flood washes a gully into a paddock. What is mainly causing this change?
items.e: The cause of this change is running water.

items.q: Which process mainly formed the sand dunes of K'gari (Fraser Island)?
c: weathering and erosion by wind and rain
items.e: Wind and waves dropped huge amounts of sand.

items.q: Waves carve a cave into the bottom of a limestone cliff. What is mainly causing this change?
items.e: The cause of this change is waves.

items.q: Which process mainly formed the Three Sisters in the Blue Mountains?
c: weathering and erosion by wind and rain
items.e: Wind and rain wore away the softer sandstone around them.

items.q: Waves wear away the bottom of a cliff and carry the pieces off. Which process is this?
items.e: Erosion picks up and removes rock pieces and soil.

items.q: Bryan wants evidence that a beach is wearing away. Which source helps most?
c: photos of the beach taken every year for 20 years
items.e: Photos over time show slow change.

items.q: Which process mainly formed the wide floodplain beside the Hawkesbury River?
items.e: Floods dropped layers of mud on the land.

items.q: A desert rock is shaped like a mushroom by sand blowing near the ground. What is mainly causing this change?
items.e: The cause of this change is wind.

items.q: A storm surge washes away the front of a sand dune at the beach. What is mainly causing this change?
items.e: The cause of this change is waves.

items.q: In the desert, rock heats up by day and cools at night until thin layers flake off. Which process is this?
items.e: Weathering breaks rock into smaller pieces where it is.

items.q: Salt crystals grow in tiny holes in a sea cliff and crumble the sandstone. Which process is this?
items.e: Weathering breaks rock into smaller pieces where it is.
